title: Rose and Martin
hook: a broom and a garden hut: the saints of Lima were both Dominican

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sermon on Hispaniola, and a question colonists didn't want to hear. Your line was are these not men. Where did you give someone back their name? Day one thousand two hundred forty.

Two objects from one city. The first is a broom. It belongs to a Dominican brother in Lima, in Peru, who uses it every day, sweeping the cloister, the infirmary, the kitchen. People in the city give him a nickname for it: Brother Broom. The second is a tiny hut at the bottom of a family garden in the same city, barely big enough to kneel in. A young woman goes there to pray among the flowers she grows and sells to help her family. The broom belonged to Martin de Porres. The hut belonged to Rose of Lima. Today, two saints, one city, and the same white habit.
screen: `A BROOM IN A PRIORY.` → `A HUT IN A FAMILY GARDEN.` → `ONE CITY, ONE WHITE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Lima under Spanish rule was a city of Spaniards, Indigenous Peruvians, Africans both enslaved and free, and people of mixed ancestry, sorted by strict lines of rank. Martin was born on the wrong side of those lines. His father was a Spanish nobleman; his mother was a free woman of African descent. When he asked to join the Dominicans, he was taken in as a helper, not as a full brother. He swept. He cut hair. He nursed the sick in the priory and in the streets, and gave away whatever came into his hands. Stories gathered around him, including his gentleness with animals, even the mice in the priory. In time the brothers received him as a lay brother. Rose took a different road to the same family. Like Catherine of Siena, the mantellata, she stayed home as a Dominican laywoman. Tradition says she took Catherine as her model. She worked with her needle and her garden to support her parents, and she made part of the house a place to care for the sick and the poor. She also practiced hard penances that can be difficult to read about today, and her biographers don't hide them. Tradition says Rose and Martin knew each other. What they share is simple. Each one found Christ in the people their city looked past. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
screen: `LIMA: A CITY SORTED BY RANK.` · `MARTIN: A HELPER, THEN A BROTHER.` · `ROSE: A LAYWOMAN AT HOME, LIKE CATHERINE.` · `CHRIST IN THE PEOPLE LIMA LOOKED PAST.` · then, large: `ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor Peru. Settle, and breathe. Bring Peru to mind, whatever you know of it: the coast and the mountains, the markets of Lima, a Peruvian neighbor, a coworker, a family who came from there, a dish you love. Hold its people for a few breaths, the ones who are struggling and the ones who are celebrating today. Then bring to mind a broom and a garden: ordinary work, offered. If you pray, you can ask Saint Rose and Saint Martin to pray for Peru, and for the people their city overlooked. If not, simply hold Peru in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Rose and Martin. Rose of Lima, a Dominican laywoman in a garden hut, and Martin de Porres, the brother with the broom: two Dominican saints of one city. Today's word.
Your line: lima's saints. Today, do one ordinary chore the way Martin swept, slowly and for someone else, and notice one person your own city tends to look past. Day one thousand two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Catholics in Peru and far beyond honor Saint Rose of Lima and Saint Martin de Porres with feast days, processions and prayers; Dominican churches in Lima keep their shrines.

trapdoor: what you thought: saints are people from a long way off and long ago.
what it means: two Dominicans in one city, a lay brother with a broom and a laywoman in a garden, who found Christ in the people Lima looked past.
what a scholar hears: Martin was the son of a Spanish nobleman and a free woman of African descent, in a city sorted by strict lines of rank.

Confirm: Martin's father Juan de Porres (Spanish nobleman) and mother Ana Velázquez (free woman of African descent, from Panama); entered the Holy Rosary priory as a donado and later professed as a lay brother.
Confirm the 'Fray Escoba' nickname and pronunciation.
Confirm Rose as a Dominican tertiary living at home, her garden hermitage, her needlework and flower-growing to support her family, and that she took Catherine of Siena as her model (tradition).
The tradition that Rose and Martin knew each other is stated as tradition; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 25:40 to confirm.
